claims.text: High-entropy nanoparticle stability is governed primarily by competition between configurational entropy and segregation forces arising from elemental surface- and cohesive-energy differences.
An initially single-phase solid solution is maintained when the net mixing enthalpy is low relative to the available thermal energy.
Otherwise, atomic diffusion triggers local ordering and phase separation.
The nanoparticles initially contain at least five metals in equal or near-equal ratios and form a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed intervention is cyclic heating from 473 K to 1923 K under a controlled inert atmosphere.
Using an inert or minimally reactive atmosphere prevents extrinsic oxidation from dominating the observed changes.
Comparable particle sizes and uniform deposition minimize morphology-induced variation.
Surface-energy disparities and cohesive-energy differences drive local chemical ordering and changes in local bonding.
Increasing operating temperature enhances atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous phase when the mixing enthalpy is low relative to atomic mobility.
Large pair-specific differences in surface or cohesive energies can cause segregation despite high configurational entropy.
The nanoparticles will largely retain a homogeneous single phase with minimal segregation up to an unspecified threshold temperature.
Above that threshold, local segregation or phase separation will occur relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
Excessively high temperatures or prolonged dwell times increase atomic mobility and may drive phase separation.
XRD, high-resolution TEM, and EDS mapping can assess phase identity, morphology, and compositional homogeneity before and after thermal cycling.
Phase separation, secondary-phase formation, or compositional gradients beyond measurement variance within the predicted stable range would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Low mixing enthalpy is said to favor stability, but the predicted outcome later attributes high-temperature segregation to mixing enthalpy becoming 'insufficient to overcome' segregation. This reverses or obscures the stated role of mixing enthalpy and does not specify its sign.

The thermodynamic framing says stability follows when thermal energy is large relative to mixing enthalpy, while the boundary implies that excessive temperature lets segregation forces overcome entropy stabilization. The distinction between temperature-driven thermodynamic stabilization and temperature-accelerated segregation kinetics is not resolved.
